note: A ratio, not a count. Absolute survivor counts rise with every
line added -- new code means new mutants, so a healthy change
with good tests would trip an absolute ratchet. The score below
is killed / (killed + survived): it stays comparable as the
codebase grows and only moves when tests get better or worse.
Not every survivor is a gap. About a quarter only change a log
or error message, which nothing asserts on by design. Others are
equivalent: `if not mismatched` decides when the read-back loop
exits, not what it returns, so killing it would mean asserting on
timing -- a worse test than the mutant is a risk.
Mutants with no covering test are excluded from the score rather
than counted as failures: the tests that drive a module through a
real subprocess load the original source, so a mutation run says
nothing about what they cover. See
docs/decisions/0005-mutation-testing-scope.md.
0.65 -> 0.67 (2026-08-19), and this is the largest rise so far,
against the largest growth so far: 2726 -> 3745 mutants, over a
0.688 -> 0.685 with 0.4.0's EQ family, and most of the fall is a
property of the measurement rather than of the tests.
`_eq_registers` alone carries 117 survivors -- the largest count of
any function in the codebase, ahead of `build_arg_parser`. Three of
them were applied by hand and run against the full suite:
prefix = None            import error, every test fails
"XX/eqXX" in the path    one test fails
tag "I" instead of "i"   one test fails
All three are killed by tests that exist. mutmut selects the tests
that *cover* a mutant from runtime coverage, and `_eq_registers`
runs at module import inside the `UCX2 = Device(...)` literal, which
is attributable to no test in particular. So the register table --
the largest body of pure data in the project -- scores as though
nothing tests it.
This is the opposite of the 0.728 problem recorded above. There the
score flattered the suite because uncovered mutants were excluded;
here it understates it because covered mutants are not attributed.
Both are reasons to read survivors rather than the number.
What reading them actually found: no new gap in the behaviour-
carrying code. The survivors in `_register_for` and
`nested_families` are `split("/", 1)` against `rsplit` or
`split("/", 2)`, which are equivalent while no path remainder has
two slashes; the rest are message text. One real looseness turned
up and was fixed: `settable_nested` answered for childless options,
so `[gain:input:3]` was rejected only by a second guard elsewhere.
0.68 -> 0.69 (2026-08-22), on the round trip for the dump's new
sections. The score rose while the code grew, which is the unusual
direction: a fixed-point test drives every branch of the renderer
over the whole register table and compares the file byte for byte,
so a mutant that survives a line-by-line assertion changes the file
The rise is measured on CI rather than locally -- see
confirmed_by_ci -- because that run is the one that exercised this
commit. The `measured` block below is still the previous commit's
local run and is the older of the two numbers; it stays until a
local run on this tree replaces it.

measured.cache: cleared before the run, as CI does

note: The measurement this min_score is set from. Ten green jobs; the
policy printed 'score rose to 0.692; raise min_score' itself,
which is what this change does.
Earlier CI runs measured below the local score (0.654 against
0.685 on afed144). This one is above it, and the difference is
the commit rather than the runner: CI ran the tree with the new
round-trip tests, the local 0.685 did not.

floor_note: The gate is min_score - tolerance = 0.68. That is the number that
matters: the score may not fall below it. min_score is set at the
measured score rounded down to the hundredth, so the policy neither
fails nor nags on the run it was recorded from -- a baseline that
prints 'raise me' on every CI run teaches people to ignore it.
Raising it is a ratchet and costs something: at 0.69 the floor is
0.68, and the last local measurement was 0.685. A change that adds
code faster than tests now has 0.005 of room on that measurement
rather than 0.015. That is the point of a ratchet, but it means the
next fall will be a failure rather than a warning.
